items.text: Internal Hom, intrinsically
The functor represented by $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(F,G)$, for $X'$ an étale space over $X$:
\operatorname{Hom}\bigl(X',\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(F,G)\bigr)=\operatorname{Hom}_{X'}\bigl(F_{X'},G_{X'}\bigr),\qquad F_{X'}=F\times X'
In $\operatorname{Top}(X)/X'$. For $X'=U$ open: the formula defining the sheaf.
=\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Top}(X)}\bigl(F\times X',\,G\bigr)
In any category with products: if this functor of $X'$ is representable, $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(F,G)$ exists. In sheaves, always.
Variants
Sheaves of groups: $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathrm{gr}}(F,G)(U)=$ group homomorphisms $F|_U\to G|_U$.
\operatorname{Hom}\bigl(X',\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathrm{gr}}(F,G)\bigr)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\text{group objects}}\bigl(F_{X'},G_{X'}\bigr)
Representable in sheaves; many variants with extra structure.
The sheaf of subsheaves
\mathcal P(F)(U)=\{\text{subsheaves of } F|_U\}
A sheaf: being a subsheaf is a local property.
$X=\mathrm{pt}$: the set of subsets of a set (Bourbaki's $\mathcal P$).
\operatorname{Hom}(X',\mathcal P(F))=\{\text{subobjects of } F\times X'\}
Subobjects in $\operatorname{Top}(X)$ or in $\operatorname{Top}(X)/X'$: same thing.
Contravariant in $X'$ by inverse image of subobjects (fibre products); representable, since being a subsheaf is local on $X'$.
Subobject classifier
Take $e=X$, the final sheaf.
\mathcal P(e)(U)=\{\text{open subsets of } U\}
\operatorname{Hom}(X',\mathcal P(e))=\operatorname{Sub}(X')
\mathcal P(F)=\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}\bigl(F,\mathcal P(e)\bigr)
In $\mathbf{Sets}$: $\mathcal P(e)=\{0,1\}$, subsets of $F$ = maps $F\to\{0,1\}$ (inverse image of one point).
Proof: both sides are the functor $X'\mapsto$ subobjects of $F\times X'$ — tautology in $\hat C$.
Topologies inside a topos
A subsheaf $\mathcal O\subset\mathcal P(F)$: for each $U$ a set $\mathcal O(U)$ of subsheaves of $F|_U$,
compatible with restriction, and local: $G\in\mathcal O(U)$ iff $G|_{U_i}\in\mathcal O(U_i)$ for a covering.
Topological space = set $F$ + subset of $\mathcal P(F)$ with two axioms. Redo it with sheaves: general topology within $\operatorname{Top}(X)$, « a space within a space ».
Caution: Hom and $\mathcal P$ and inverse images
Unlike finite limits, they do not commute with $f^*$. Only canonical arrows:
f^*\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(F,G)\longrightarrow\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(f^*F,f^*G)
f^*\mathcal P(F)\longrightarrow\mathcal P(f^*F)
Not isomorphisms in general (e.g. a fibre functor); they are when $f$ is étale.
$f^*$ and infinite products
$f^*$ does not commute with infinite inverse limits, e.g. products.
\Bigl(\prod_i F_i\Bigr)_x\longrightarrow\prod_i (F_i)_x
Injective? Two families $f_i,g_i$ agreeing near $x$, on neighbourhoods $U_i$ depending on $i$.
Counterexample if $x$ is not isolated: $F_i=$ the sheaf of maps $X\to E$, $E$ with two points.
U_0\supset U_1\supset\cdots\ni x,\quad f_i\equiv a,\quad g_i=a\ \text{on } U_i,\ g_i=b\ \text{off } U_i
Injective iff $x$ has a smallest open neighbourhood (isolated point in a separated space).
Infinite products of epimorphisms
In $\mathbf{Sets}$ a product of surjections is surjective. Not in sheaves.
F_i\twoheadrightarrow G_i\ \ \not\Longrightarrow\ \ \prod F_i\to\prod G_i\ \text{epi}
Reduce to $G_i=e$ (inverse images commute with products of sections): is $\prod F_i\to e$ epi when each $F_i\to e$ is?
Each $F_i$ has a section on some $U_i\ni x$; need a common neighbourhood.
U_i\ \text{nbhds of } x,\quad \bigcap_i U_i\ \text{not a neighbourhood of } x
Take $F_i=U_i\sqcup(X\smallsetminus\{x\})$: étale, covers $X$, but no section of the product near $x$.
With some connectedness assumed (line, plane): works at any non-isolated point.
$X$ compact, totally disconnected: epi of sheaves iff $F(U)\to G(U)$ onto for all $U$, so products of epis are epis.
Conversely: products of epis always epi $\Rightarrow$ disjoint closed sets separated by an open-closed set. Total disconnectedness.
Space from category of sheaves
Aim: topological notions expressed in $\operatorname{Top}(X)$, in a natural way.
Objection: sheaves of sets are « silly »? Sheaves of groups, rings... are recovered from $\operatorname{Top}(X)$.
Connectedness
X\ \text{connected}\iff\bigl(X=X_1\sqcup X_2,\ X_i\ \text{open}\Rightarrow X_1=\varnothing\ \text{or}\ X_2=\varnothing\bigr)
Put $E=\operatorname{Top}(X)$; $X$ is its final object $e$.
e\ \text{is not a direct sum of two non-initial subobjects of } e
